label: Survival Mandarin
blurb: The phrases you need in your first weeks — by ear and meaning, no reading required.
blurbZh: 剛到台灣前幾週最需要的那些話。只靠聽和意思，不需要認字。

questions.q: Someone you have just met says 你好. They are —
questions.why: 你好 (nǐ hǎo) is the all-purpose hello. Safe with anyone, any time of day.

questions.q: Walking into the office at 7:40 a.m., you greet colleagues with —
questions.why: 早安 (zǎo'ān) is good morning. Many people shorten it to just 早 (zǎo) — one syllable, and completely normal.

questions.q: A colleague hands you a coffee. You say —
questions.why: 謝謝 (xièxie) is thank you, and it is the most useful word on this list. Use it freely — it is never too much.

questions.q: Someone thanks you. You reply —
questions.why: 不客氣 (bú kèqi) — you're welcome. Note the tone: 不 rises here, bú, because 客 falls.

questions.q: You step on someone's foot in the corridor. You say —
questions.why: 對不起 (duìbùqǐ) is a real apology — you did something. For the lighter excuse-me when squeezing past, 不好意思 is the usual choice.

questions.q: Someone apologizes for a small mistake. You reassure them with —
questions.why: 沒關係 (méi guānxi) — it doesn't matter, no harm done. The standard reply to an apology.

questions.q: You need to squeeze past someone in a narrow corridor. You say —
questions.why: 不好意思 (bù hǎoyìsi) is the everyday excuse-me — passing someone, interrupting, asking a small favor. Lighter than 對不起.

questions.q: You are leaving the office at the end of the day. You say —
questions.why: 再見 (zàijiàn) is goodbye. Colleagues often say 掰掰 (bāibāi) too — the same word English lent them.

questions.q: Listen. A shopkeeper says this as you leave. It means —
questions.why: 慢走 (màn zǒu) literally walks slowly — said to someone leaving, as a small kindness. You are not expected to reply with anything but a nod.

questions.q: Listen. A colleague says this at the end of a long day. They mean —
opts: that was hard work, thank you
questions.why: 辛苦了 (xīnkǔ le) acknowledges someone's effort. There is no neat English equivalent; thanks for your hard work is the closest.

questions.q: Listen. Students shout this at a sports day. It means —
opts: go on, you can do it
questions.why: 加油 (jiāyóu) literally add oil — the all-purpose cheer. You will hear it at sports day, before exams, and whenever anyone needs encouragement.

questions.q: You are about to ask a stranger for directions. You open with —
questions.why: 請問 (qǐngwèn) — may I ask. It signals a question is coming and makes it polite before you have said anything else.

questions.q: A student asks you 你叫什麼名字. They want —
questions.why: 你叫什麼名字 (nǐ jiào shénme míngzi) — what is your name. Answer with 我叫 (wǒ jiào) and your name.

questions.q: You want to tell someone your name. You start with —
questions.why: 我叫 (wǒ jiào) — I am called. 我是 (wǒ shì) also works and is slightly more formal; either is fine.

questions.q: Meeting your co-teacher for the first time, you can add —
opts: 我先走了 (wǒ xiān zǒu le)
很高興認識你 (hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ)
questions.why: 很高興認識你 (hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ) — pleased to meet you. Worth learning whole; you will use it on your first day at every school.

questions.q: Someone proposes a time to meet and you agree. The shortest reply is —
questions.why: 好 (hǎo) on its own means fine / OK / agreed. One syllable, and it carries an enormous amount of daily conversation.

questions.q: Listen. Someone confirms what you said. They are saying —
questions.why: 對 (duì) — correct, right, yes. Its opposite is 不對 (bú duì). Taiwanese Mandarin leans on 對 the way English leans on yeah.

questions.q: A student asks you something you genuinely cannot answer. You say —
questions.why: 我不知道 (wǒ bù zhīdào) — I don't know. Perfectly acceptable to say; adding 我問一下 (wǒ wèn yíxià), I'll go ask, makes it better.

questions.q: Listen. Someone greets you with this. They are asking —
questions.why: 你好嗎 (nǐ hǎo ma) — how are you. Less common between Taiwanese colleagues than textbooks suggest; 吃飽了嗎 or a simple nod is more usual.

questions.q: Someone asks how you are and you are fine. You answer —
questions.why: 我很好 (wǒ hěn hǎo) — I'm well. 很 is almost obligatory here; 我好 on its own sounds unfinished.

questions.q: Listen. What is starting?
questions.why: 上課 (shàngkè) — class begins. Its opposite, 下課 (xiàkè), is the bell you will learn fastest.

questions.q: Listen. What has just happened?
questions.why: 下課 (xiàkè) — class is over. Ten minutes between periods, and the corridor will tell you before the word does.

questions.q: Listen. A class says this in unison as you walk in. It is —
questions.why: 老師好 (lǎoshī hǎo) — good day, teacher. Classes often say it standing, all together, at the start of a lesson. A nod back is enough.

questions.q: Listen. The class monitor calls this. The students —
questions.why: 起立 (qǐlì) — stand. Part of the opening routine in many classes: 起立, greeting, 坐下. The monitor leads it, not you.

questions.q: Listen. The class monitor calls this. The students —
questions.why: 坐下 (zuò xià) — sit down. The other half of the opening routine.

questions.q: You need the class to quieten down. The word for quiet is —
questions.why: 安靜 (ānjìng) — quiet. Said firmly, once, it works; said repeatedly it stops meaning anything, the same as in English.

questions.q: You want the class to listen to you. You say —
questions.why: 聽我說 (tīng wǒ shuō) — listen to me. Pairs naturally with 看這裡, look over here.

questions.q: You want everyone's eyes on the board. You say —
questions.why: 看這裡 (kàn zhèlǐ) — look here. Point as you say it and even a class with no English will follow.

questions.q: Listen. You would say this when you want students to —
questions.why: 跟我念 (gēn wǒ niàn) — read after me. The single most useful instruction in a language classroom.

questions.q: Listen. A student has answered correctly and you say this. It means —
questions.why: 很好 (hěn hǎo) — very good. 好棒 (hǎo bàng) is warmer and very common with younger children.

questions.q: A student is answering too quietly. You ask for —
questions.why: 大聲一點 (dàshēng yìdiǎn) — a bit louder. The pattern 一點 after an adjective means a bit more of it.

questions.q: You want the class to do it one more time. You say —
questions.why: 再一次 (zài yí cì) — once more. 再 means again; you will meet it constantly.

questions.q: Listen. A colleague says this as a child runs past with scissors. It means —
questions.why: 小心 (xiǎoxīn) — careful. One of the few words worth being able to say instantly, without thinking.

questions.q: You are pointing at a worksheet and want the student to write their name. The word you need is —
questions.why: 你的名字 (nǐ de míngzi) — your name. 的 (de) links owner to thing, like apostrophe-s.

questions.q: Listen. A student is asking where they left their —
questions.why: 課本 (kèběn) — textbook. 課 is lesson and 本 is the measure word for books.

questions.q: Listen. A student is asking to borrow a —
questions.why: 鉛筆 (qiānbǐ) — pencil. 筆 covers writing implements generally, so 原子筆 is a ballpoint.

questions.q: Listen. The homeroom teacher is talking about —
questions.why: 作業 (zuòyè) — homework. If you hear it with 交 (jiāo), someone is talking about handing it in.

questions.q: Listen. What is being discussed?
questions.why: 考試 (kǎoshì) — a test or exam. The bigger termly one is 段考 (duànkǎo), and regular lessons often pause around it.

questions.q: Listen. They are talking about the —
questions.why: 教室 (jiàoshì) — classroom. Note the tone on 教 here: jiào, the same as in 教育.

questions.q: A colleague is struggling with a stack of books. You offer help with —
questions.why: 我來 (wǒ lái) — let me. Two syllables that make you useful; reach for the books as you say it.

questions.q: Listen. The schedule shows this at 7:50. Expect —
questions.why: 朝會 (zhāohuì) — morning assembly, usually on the playground. Note the reading: zhāo, morning, not cháo.

questions.q: Listen. Around 12:40 this happens. It is —
questions.why: 午休 (wǔxiū) — the lunchtime rest. Lights off, heads on desks, and the whole school observes it at once. Do not schedule anything into it.

questions.q: Listen. Students fetch brooms. It is —
questions.why: 打掃時間 (dǎsǎo shíjiān) — cleaning time. Students clean the school as part of their education, not as punishment. Joining in occasionally is noticed.

questions.q: Listen. What is happening at 4 p.m.?
questions.why: 放學 (fàngxué) — school lets out. Different from 下課, which is just the end of one period.

questions.q: Listen. What is about to happen?
questions.why: 升旗 (shēngqí) — the flag raising. A whole-school routine; teachers stand with their classes rather than staying in the office.

questions.q: Someone says your class is 第一節. That means —
questions.why: 第一節 (dì yī jié) — first period. 第 turns a number into an ordinal; 節 is the measure word for class periods.

questions.q: You want to know what time something starts. You ask —
questions.why: 幾點 (jǐ diǎn) — what time. Expect the answer as a number plus 點; you may need it repeated, which is fine.

questions.q: Listen. 今天 means —
questions.why: 今天 (jīntiān) — today. With 明天 (tomorrow) and 昨天 (yesterday) you can place most things people tell you.

questions.q: Listen. When is it happening?
questions.why: 明天 (míngtiān) — tomorrow. If you catch only this word in a sentence, you already know when to worry.

questions.q: Listen. What is happening?
questions.why: 開會 (kāihuì) — to have a meeting. If you hear it with a time attached, that time is probably yours too.

questions.q: You need to be away on Friday. The word for taking leave is —
questions.why: 請假 (qǐngjià) — to request leave. Tell the office early; the paperwork usually goes through 人事室.

questions.q: Listen. A colleague is saying they are —
questions.why: 下班 (xiàbān) — to finish work, the adult version of 放學. 上班 is its opposite.

questions.q: Listen. Which day is it?
questions.why: 星期一 (xīngqíyī) — Monday. The days run 星期一 through 星期六 by number, and Sunday is 星期日 or 星期天.

questions.q: Listen. They are talking about the —
questions.why: 週末 (zhōumò) — weekend. Worth knowing alongside 補課日, a Saturday worked to bridge a long weekend.

questions.q: Listen. What event is being planned?
questions.why: 運動會 (yùndònghuì) — sports day. A whole-school event that usually rearranges the timetable for days around it.

questions.q: Listen. The class is going on —
questions.why: 校外教學 (xiàowài jiàoxué) — a school outing. Your lesson that day is almost certainly canceled rather than moved.

questions.q: You need someone to wait a moment. You say —
questions.why: 等一下 (děng yíxià) — wait a moment. Also used as in a minute when someone asks you to do something now.

questions.q: The class is moving too slowly. You ask them to —
questions.why: 快一點 (kuài yìdiǎn) — a bit faster. Same 一點 pattern as 大聲一點 and 慢一點.

questions.q: You are leaving the office before your colleagues. You say —
opts: 我先走了 (wǒ xiān zǒu le)
questions.why: 我先走了 (wǒ xiān zǒu le) — I'll head off first. Saying it as you leave is a small courtesy that is noticed when it is missing.

questions.q: You are leaving and will see them tomorrow. You say —
questions.why: 明天見 (míngtiān jiàn) — see you tomorrow. Swap in any time word: 下禮拜見, 星期一見.

questions.q: At a food stall you want to know the price. You ask —
questions.why: 多少錢 (duōshǎo qián) — how much. Expect the answer as a number you may not catch; a calculator or their fingers usually follows.

questions.q: You cannot name the dish, so you point at it and say —
questions.why: 這個 (zhège) — this one. Point and say it, and you can order anything without knowing a single food word.

questions.q: You are ordering and want to say I'd like. You start with —
questions.why: 我要 (wǒ yào) — I want. Blunter than English I'd like, but completely normal when ordering.

questions.q: You are vegetarian and want to say so before ordering. You say —
questions.why: 我吃素 (wǒ chīsù) — I'm vegetarian. Widely understood in Taiwan, where 素食 is common and well catered for.

questions.q: You want your food without chili. You say —
questions.why: 不要辣 (bú yào là) — no chili. The same pattern works for anything: 不要 plus the thing you do not want.

questions.q: You cannot stand coriander. You say —
questions.why: 不要香菜 (bú yào xiāngcài) — no coriander. Worth memorizing if you are one of the people for whom it tastes of soap.

questions.q: Listen. The counter staff is asking whether you want —
questions.why: 內用 (nèiyòng) — eat in. Its pair is 外帶, take away; you will be asked this at almost every counter.

questions.q: Listen. The counter staff is asking whether you want —
questions.why: 外帶 (wàidài) — take away. Answering with just the word, 外帶, is a complete and natural reply.

questions.q: Listen. Your colleague is offering to order you a —
questions.why: 便當 (biàndāng) — a boxed meal, the staple school lunch. Someone will often collect orders for the whole office.

questions.q: Listen. They are saying the food is —
questions.why: 好吃 (hǎochī) — tasty, of food. For drinks it is 好喝 (hǎohē). Saying it to whoever fed you is always well received.

questions.q: Your colleague brings you tea and it is excellent. You say —
questions.why: 好喝 (hǎohē) — good to drink. The 好 + verb pattern runs through 好看 (good-looking) and 好聽 (nice to hear) as well.

questions.q: There is something you cannot eat. You say —
questions.why: 我不吃 (wǒ bù chī) — I don't eat that. Add the thing in front for clarity: 牛肉我不吃.

questions.q: You want just a small amount. You say —
questions.why: 一點點 (yìdiǎndiǎn) — just a little. Useful for declining most of something without refusing it outright.

questions.q: Listen. Someone offers you a bag and you decline. They heard —
questions.why: 不用 (bú yòng) — no need, don't bother. Gentler than 不要 and the usual way to turn down an offer.

questions.q: Listen. You have enough. This means —
questions.why: 好了 (hǎo le) — that's it, done, enough. Said while someone is pouring or serving, it means stop there.

questions.q: You are ready to pay at a restaurant. You say —
questions.why: 結帳 (jiézhàng) — to settle the bill. In smaller places you take the slip to the counter rather than wait at the table.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking whether you will pay with —
questions.why: 現金 (xiànjīn) — cash. Many small stalls still take nothing else, so carry some.

questions.q: Listen. They are handing you a —
questions.why: 發票 (fāpiào) — the official receipt, which doubles as a lottery ticket in Taiwan. Worth keeping.

questions.q: Listen. A colleague greets you with this at noon. They are —
questions.why: 吃飽了嗎 (chī bǎo le ma) — have you eaten. Often just a greeting rather than a real question; 吃飽了, 謝謝 closes it politely.

questions.q: Listen. Your colleague says this at the register. They mean —
questions.why: 我請客 (wǒ qǐngkè) — my treat. Accepting graciously is the right move; you return it another day rather than insisting now.

questions.q: You did not understand what was just said. You say —
questions.why: 我不懂 (wǒ bù dǒng) — I don't understand. Nobody minds hearing it; what causes trouble is nodding when you did not follow.

questions.q: You want someone to repeat what they said. You say —
opts: 我先走了 (wǒ xiān zǒu le)
請再說一次 (qǐng zài shuō yí cì)
questions.why: 請再說一次 (qǐng zài shuō yí cì) — please say it once more. Pair it with 慢一點 and you can get through most conversations.

questions.q: Someone is speaking too fast for you. You ask for —
questions.why: 慢一點 (màn yìdiǎn) — a bit slower. More useful than asking for English, because it keeps you in the conversation.

questions.q: You are stuck and want to know if they speak English. You ask —
opts: 你是老師嗎 (nǐ shì lǎoshī ma)
你會說英文嗎 (nǐ huì shuō Yīngwén ma)
questions.why: 你會說英文嗎 (nǐ huì shuō Yīngwén ma) — do you speak English. Ask it in Mandarin and the answer comes more readily than if you open in English.

questions.q: You want to warn someone your Mandarin is weak. You say —
opts: 我的中文不好 (wǒ de Zhōngwén bù hǎo)
我不是老師 (wǒ bú shì lǎoshī)
questions.why: 我的中文不好 (wǒ de Zhōngwén bù hǎo) — my Chinese isn't good. Saying it in Mandarin tends to produce warm disagreement and slower speech.

questions.q: You are pointing at something unfamiliar. You ask —
questions.why: 這是什麼 (zhè shì shénme) — what is this. With a pointing finger it works on food, forms and machinery alike.

questions.q: You want to know how to say a word in Mandarin. You ask —
questions.why: 怎麼說 (zěnme shuō) — how do you say it. Point at the thing and ask; you will collect vocabulary faster this way than from any list.

questions.q: Listen. Someone says this when a problem appears. They mean —
questions.why: 怎麼辦 (zěnme bàn) — what do we do now. You will hear it whenever something goes wrong.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking —
questions.why: 為什麼 (wèishénme) — why. Recognizing the question word tells you what kind of answer is wanted, even if you miss the rest.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking —
questions.why: 誰 (shéi) — who. Also pronounced shuí in more formal speech; shéi is what you will hear day to day.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking —
questions.why: 什麼時候 (shénme shíhòu) — when. Longer than 幾點 and asks about the occasion rather than the clock time.

questions.q: You want to check whether something is allowed. You ask —
questions.why: 可以嗎 (kěyǐ ma) — is that OK / may I. Add it to the end of almost anything to turn it into a polite request.

questions.q: Listen. You asked permission and they replied this. It means —
questions.why: 可以 (kěyǐ) — you may, that works. 不可以 is its refusal.

questions.q: Listen. You asked permission and they replied this. It means —
questions.why: 不行 (bùxíng) — no, that's not on. Firmer than 不可以 and rarely softened, so take it at face value.

questions.q: You want to say there is a problem. You say —
questions.why: 有問題 (yǒu wèntí) — there's a problem, or I have a question. Context does the work; the words are the same.

questions.q: Listen. You asked for help and they replied this. It means —
questions.why: 沒問題 (méi wèntí) — no problem, consider it done. 沒 negates 有 the way 不 negates most other verbs.

questions.q: You need someone to help you. You say —
questions.why: 幫我 (bāng wǒ) — help me. Adding 一下 softens it: 幫我一下, give me a hand.

questions.q: Listen. Someone opens a request with this. They are —
questions.why: 麻煩你 (máfan nǐ) — sorry to trouble you. A softener at the front of a request; hearing it means one is coming.

questions.q: You forgot something you were asked to do. You say —
questions.why: 我忘了 (wǒ wàng le) — I forgot. Followed by 對不起 it is a complete and acceptable apology.

questions.q: You are not sure you can do it but you will try. You say —
questions.why: 我試試看 (wǒ shìshi kàn) — I'll give it a go. Doubling the verb makes it tentative and modest, which lands well here.

questions.q: Listen. Which number?
questions.why: 一 (yī) — one. On its own it is first tone; in 一個 it shifts to yí, and in 一起 to yì. Your ear will pick this up before any rule does.

questions.q: Listen. Which number?
questions.why: 二 (èr) — two. When counting things you usually say 兩 (liǎng) instead: 兩個, two of them.

questions.q: Listen. Which number?
questions.why: 三 (sān) — three. First tone, flat and level.

questions.q: Listen. Which number?
questions.why: 五 (wǔ) — five. Third tone, the one that dips and rises.

questions.q: Listen. Which number?
questions.why: 十 (shí) — ten. Numbers above ten build from it: 十一 is eleven, 二十 is twenty.

questions.q: Listen. How much?
questions.why: 一百 (yìbǎi) — one hundred. Prices at food stalls live between 一百 and 兩百, so this is the one to recognize fast.

questions.q: You want two of something. You say —
questions.why: 兩個 (liǎng ge) — two of them. Use 兩 not 二 when counting; 個 is the general-purpose measure word that works when you do not know the right one.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking —
questions.why: 幾個 (jǐ ge) — how many. 幾 expects a small number; 多少 is for larger or open amounts.

questions.q: Listen. What time?
questions.why: 八點 (bā diǎn) — eight o'clock. 點 marks the hour; 半 after it makes it half past.

questions.q: Listen. What time?
questions.why: 三點半 (sān diǎn bàn) — half past three. 半 is half, and it always follows the hour.

questions.q: Listen. Which part of the day?
questions.why: 早上 (zǎoshang) — morning. With 下午 (afternoon) and 晚上 (evening) you can place any time someone gives you.

questions.q: Listen. Which part of the day?
questions.why: 下午 (xiàwǔ) — afternoon. Times are said with the part of day first: 下午三點, three in the afternoon.

questions.q: Listen. Which part of the day?
questions.why: 晚上 (wǎnshang) — evening. A staff dinner will almost always be 晚上.

questions.q: The price is more than you want to pay. You say —
questions.why: 太貴了 (tài guì le) — too expensive. The 太⋯了 frame works with any adjective: 太辣了, 太吵了.

questions.q: At a market you would like a better price. You say —
questions.why: 便宜一點 (piányí yìdiǎn) — a bit cheaper. Fine at a night market or a traditional market; not at a convenience store.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking whether you have —
questions.why: 零錢 (língqián) — loose change. Small stalls often ask, because breaking a large note is genuinely inconvenient for them.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking whether you want to —
questions.why: 刷卡 (shuākǎ) — to pay by card. 可以刷卡嗎 is how you ask whether they take one.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking for your —
questions.why: 悠遊卡 (yōuyóu kǎ) — the EasyCard, used on buses, trains and in convenience stores. Worth getting in your first week.

questions.q: Listen. The sign says this. It means there is —
questions.why: 打折 (dǎzhé) — a discount. Taiwanese discounts count down: 八折 is 20% off, not 80% off.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking for your —
questions.why: 號碼 (hàomǎ) — number, as in a phone number or a queue ticket. 電話號碼 is a phone number.

questions.q: Listen. What are they asking about?
questions.why: 廁所 (cèsuǒ) — the toilet. 廁所在哪裡 (cèsuǒ zài nǎlǐ) is worth memorizing whole.

questions.q: You are looking for a place and want to ask where it is. You use —
questions.why: 在哪裡 (zài nǎlǐ) — where is it. Put the place in front: 廁所在哪裡, 辦公室在哪裡.

questions.q: Listen. They are directing you to the —
questions.why: 辦公室 (bàngōngshì) — office. Teachers in Taiwanese schools share a staffroom rather than having their own rooms.

questions.q: Listen. A child is being sent to the —
questions.why: 健康中心 (jiànkāng zhōngxīn) — the nurse's room, also called 保健室. Where you send a student who is hurt or unwell.

questions.q: Listen. Which room?
questions.why: 圖書館 (túshūguǎn) — library. 館 marks a building for a purpose: 體育館 is the sports hall.

questions.q: Listen. Where is the assembly held?
questions.why: 操場 (cāochǎng) — the playground or running track. Morning assembly and sports day both happen here.

questions.q: Listen. The room is —
questions.why: 樓上 (lóushàng) — upstairs. Its pair is 樓下, downstairs. Taiwanese schools count the ground floor as 一樓.

questions.q: Listen. Which floor?
questions.why: 三樓 (sān lóu) — third floor. Numbers plus 樓 give you any floor; note that 一樓 is the ground floor.

questions.q: Listen. Which side?
questions.why: 右邊 (yòubiān) — the right side. Its pair is 左邊. Directions usually come with a pointing hand, which helps.

questions.q: Listen. Which side?
questions.why: 左邊 (zuǒbiān) — the left side. 邊 means side and attaches to most position words.

questions.q: Listen. You should —
questions.why: 直走 (zhí zǒu) — go straight. Combined with 左轉 and 右轉, turn left and right, this covers most directions you will be given.

questions.q: Listen. They mean —
questions.why: 這裡 (zhèlǐ) — here. Its pair is 那裡, there. The same 這 / 那 split runs through 這個 and 那個.

questions.q: Listen. The place is —
questions.why: 很近 (hěn jìn) — close by. 很遠 (hěn yuǎn) is its opposite, and in Taiwan 很近 often still means a ten-minute walk.

questions.q: Listen. They are suggesting you —
questions.why: 走路 (zǒulù) — to go on foot. 走路去 means walk there.

questions.q: Listen. They are telling you to take the —
questions.why: 公車 (gōngchē) — public bus. 火車 is the train and 高鐵 the high-speed rail.

questions.q: Listen. Where are they going?
questions.why: 火車站 (huǒchē zhàn) — train station. 站 means station or stop, so 公車站 is a bus stop.

questions.q: Listen. They are talking about a —
questions.why: 機車 (jīchē) — scooter, the default way to get around Changhua. Note it does not mean machine car.

questions.q: Listen. They are telling you where to —
questions.why: 停車 (tíngchē) — to park. 停車場 is the car park; most schools have a marked area for scooters.

questions.q: Listen. They are pointing you to a —
questions.why: 便利商店 (biànlì shāngdiàn) — convenience store. Usually just called by the brand; they handle parcels, bills and tickets as well as food.

questions.q: Listen. Where are they going?
questions.why: 郵局 (yóujú) — post office. Also where many people keep a savings account, so the queue may not be about parcels.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 老師 (lǎoshī) — teacher, and also how people will address you, often with your surname in front.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 校長 (xiàozhǎng) — the principal. Note the reading of 長 here: zhǎng, head of something, not cháng.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 主任 (zhǔrèn) — director, the head of one of the school offices. Above 組長 and below 校長.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 學生 (xuéshēng) — student. 學 is to study and appears in 學校, 大學, 同學.

questions.q: Listen. A teacher is addressing the —
questions.why: 同學 (tóngxué) — classmate, and the normal way a teacher addresses students as a group or one by one.

questions.q: Listen. Who is coming to the school?
questions.why: 家長 (jiāzhǎng) — parent or guardian. Again 長 is zhǎng; 家長會 is the parents' association.

questions.q: Listen. Who should you speak to about one student?
questions.why: 導師 (dǎoshī) — homeroom teacher, often shortened to 班導. Your first stop for anything about a particular child.

questions.q: Listen. Who is being called?
questions.why: 護理師 (hùlǐshī) — the school nurse, who staffs the 健康中心. The older word 護士 is still heard.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 外師 (wàishī) — foreign teacher, short for 外籍教師. This is you, in almost every staffroom conversation.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they talking about?
questions.why: 同事 (tóngshì) — colleague. The 同 prefix means fellow: 同學, 同事, 同鄉.

questions.q: Listen. Who are they referring to?
questions.why: 他 (tā) — he, she or it. Spoken Mandarin makes no gender distinction here, which trips up new listeners constantly.

questions.q: Listen. Who is included?
questions.why: 我們 (wǒmen) — we, us. 們 marks a plural person: 你們, 他們.

questions.q: Listen. Who is being addressed?
questions.why: 你們 (nǐmen) — you, plural. Useful when giving instructions to a whole class.

questions.q: You found a lost water bottle and want to know whose it is. You ask —
questions.why: 誰的 (shéi de) — whose. Hold the object up as you ask and the class will sort it out.

questions.q: A visitor comes into the staffroom. You offer a seat with —
questions.why: 請坐 (qǐng zuò) — please sit. 請 in front of a verb makes it a polite request.

questions.q: Listen. Someone knocks and you say this. You are telling them to —
questions.why: 請進 (qǐng jìn) — come in. The reply when someone knocks on the staffroom door.

questions.q: Listen. You are being told that —
questions.why: 等一下他來 (děng yíxià tā lái) — he'll be here in a moment. 等一下 works as in a minute as well as wait.

questions.q: Listen. The person you are looking for —
questions.why: 他不在 (tā bú zài) — he's not in. 在 means to be present; 不在 is the standard answer at an office door.

questions.q: Listen. Walking into an office, you are asked —
questions.why: 你找誰 (nǐ zhǎo shéi) — who are you looking for. Answer with 我找 plus the name or the role.

questions.q: You are looking for a particular colleague. You start with —
questions.why: 我找 (wǒ zhǎo) — I'm looking for. Follow it with a name or a title: 我找王老師.

questions.q: You are feeling unwell and need to say so. You say —
questions.why: 我不舒服 (wǒ bù shūfú) — I don't feel well. The usual way to open a conversation about sick leave.

questions.q: Listen. They are suggesting you —
questions.why: 看醫生 (kàn yīshēng) — to see a doctor. Clinics are everywhere and walk-in; your 健保卡 keeps it cheap.

questions.q: Listen. Where should you go?
questions.why: 藥局 (yàojú) — pharmacy. For minor things a pharmacist will often sort you out without a clinic visit.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking for your —
questions.why: 健保卡 (jiànbǎo kǎ) — National Health Insurance card. Carry it; without it a clinic visit costs several times more.

questions.q: Listen. What is the weather doing?
questions.why: 下雨 (xiàyǔ) — raining. 下 is used for things that come down: 下雨, 下雪.

questions.q: Listen. They are saying it is —
questions.why: 很熱 (hěn rè) — very hot. From May to September this is small talk, not information.

questions.q: Listen. What is coming?
questions.why: 颱風 (táifēng) — typhoon. Whether school closes is announced by the county, not your principal, usually the evening before.

questions.q: Listen. What just happened?
questions.why: 地震 (dìzhèn) — earthquake. Small ones are routine in Taiwan; your students will be calmer than you are.

questions.q: Listen. Tomorrow is —
questions.why: 放假 (fàngjià) — a holiday, a day off. 補課日 is its opposite: a Saturday worked to bridge a long weekend.

questions.q: You are asked to join something but cannot. You say —
questions.why: 我沒空 (wǒ méi kòng) — I'm not free. Softer than 我不要, which can sound blunt to the point of rude.

questions.q: Listen. They are suggesting —
questions.why: 下次 (xiàcì) — next time. Declining with 下次好嗎 keeps the door open, which matters more here than a clean no.

questions.q: Someone calls you and you are on your way. You answer —
questions.why: 我來了 (wǒ lái le) — coming. 了 marks the change: it was not happening, now it is.

questions.q: Listen. They are telling you they have —
questions.why: 我到了 (wǒ dào le) — I've arrived. Useful when someone is waiting for you.

questions.q: You need a moment before someone leaves. You say —
questions.why: 等我 (děng wǒ) — wait for me. Add 一下 to soften it into just a second.

questions.q: You need someone to pass you something. You say —
questions.why: 給我 (gěi wǒ) — give me. On its own it is blunt; 請給我 or adding 一下 makes it a request.

questions.q: Listen. They are saying they —
questions.why: 沒有 (méiyǒu) — there isn't, I don't have. The negative of 有, and one of the most common words you will hear.

questions.q: Listen. They are confirming that they —
questions.why: 有 (yǒu) — to have, there is. Asking 有沒有 plus a thing is how you ask whether something exists or is in stock.

questions.q: Listen. They are asking —
questions.why: 真的嗎 (zhēnde ma) — really? An all-purpose reaction; 真的 on its own means genuinely, truly.

questions.q: Listen. They are reacting to good news with —
questions.why: 太好了 (tài hǎo le) — that's wonderful. Same 太⋯了 frame as 太貴了, but this one is delight rather than complaint.

questions.q: Listen. Someone says this as you leave feeling unwell. It means —
questions.why: 保重 (bǎozhòng) — look after yourself. Warmer than 再見 and used when someone is unwell or going away for a while.
